```{r}
#| include: false

library(glue)
library(ggthemes)
library(ggrepel)
library(broom)
library(av)
library(ggridges)
library(gganimate)
library(gt)
library(quantreg)
library(tidyverse)


#----------------------------------- 
########## Overall structure of speed / efficiency issues: saving / caching
#----------------------------------- 
# Particularly because of bootstrapping, there are speed issues during local testing
# labeled sections with "fit-model-"
# these save models .rds into the folder (always using set.seed(123) and num_boot_sim <- 600)
# set to eval: false; just need to manually re-run if there are updates to those sections or data
# otherwise, subsequent sections using the model just load the saved .rds from folders rather than recreate it each time 

# similar approach for video creations of animated graphs
# cache is another option, but within Quarto may be a bit opaque, may be a easier to just set chunks as not evaluating


#----------------------------------- 
########## Quantile regression
#----------------------------------- 
# For initial testing/working through might use 200 for speed/efficiency;
# When finalizing, better to use 600+
num_boot_sim <- 600


#----------------------------------- 
########## Data load, contains all years
#----------------------------------- 
dfsquads_1930_2026 <- readRDS("data_prepared/dfsquads_final_1930_2026.rds") %>% 
  # For graphing purposes, I like them in this order
  mutate(squad_position_name = 
           factor(squad_position_name,
                  levels = c("goal keeper", "defender", 
                             "midfielder", "forward"), 
                  labels = c("Goal keeper", "Defender", 
                             "Midfielder", "Forward"),
                  ordered = TRUE))

#----------------------------------- 
########## Data filtering for primary analysis
#----------------------------------- 
# Expansion era of 1982 onwards
year_start <- 1982

dfsquads <- dfsquads_1930_2026 %>% 
  filter(year >= year_start) %>% 
  mutate(Years.Since.1982 = year - 1982, 
       # Nice to show meaningful coefficients, center year at start
       team_year_cluster = paste0(year, "_", team_code)) 

#----------------------------------- 
########## Apperances for follow up analysis
#----------------------------------- 
# core cut off
core_team_cutoff <- 15

df_squads_appearances <- dfsquads %>% 
  left_join(
    # data to join: calculating appearances
    wc_apperances <- dfsquads_1930_2026 %>% 
      distinct(year, team_code) %>% 
      arrange(team_code, year) %>% 
      group_by(team_code) %>% 
      mutate(first_appearance = ifelse(row_number() == 1, TRUE, FALSE),
             count_appearances = row_number(),
             total_appearances = n()),
    # joining by team code not name 
    by = join_by(year, team_code)
  ) %>% 
  mutate(core_team = total_appearances >= core_team_cutoff,
         non_core_team = total_appearances < core_team_cutoff)


#----------------------------------- 
########## Setting colors
#----------------------------------- 
# paletteer::paletteer_d("RColorBrewer::Set1")
# paletteer::paletteer_d("RColorBrewer::Spectral")

palette_red <- "#E41A1CFF"
palette_blue <- "#377EB8FF"
palette_green <- "#4DAF4AFF"
palette_purple <- "#984EA3FF"
  

#----------------------------------- 
########## Age over time, Summary for Initial Visuals
#----------------------------------- 
### summarydf used for visuals, 
  # so choosing names for display rather than tidy name formats
summarydf <- dfsquads %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarize(
    Mean = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE),
    Median = median(age, na.rm = TRUE),
    SD   = sd(age, na.rm = TRUE),
    IQR = IQR(age, na.rm = TRUE),
    Min  = min(age, na.rm = TRUE),
    Max  = max(age, na.rm = TRUE),
    `99th` = quantile(age, probs = .99, na.rm = TRUE),
    `95th` = quantile(age, probs = .95, na.rm = TRUE),
    `90th` = quantile(age, probs = .90, na.rm = TRUE),
    `85th` = quantile(age, probs = .85, na.rm = TRUE),
    `80th` = quantile(age, probs = .80, na.rm = TRUE),
    # any movement on the lower end?
    `20th` = quantile(age, probs = .20, na.rm = TRUE),
    `15th` = quantile(age, probs = .15, na.rm = TRUE),
    `10th` = quantile(age, probs = .10, na.rm = TRUE),
    `05th` = quantile(age, probs = .05, na.rm = TRUE),
    `01st` = quantile(age, probs = .01, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) 

# Range across measures of interest
  # to aid in plotting on scales with comparable ranges
limits_df <- summarydf %>%
  pivot_longer(
    -year,
  ) %>% 
  filter(!name %in% c("SD", "IQR")) %>% 
  group_by(name) %>%
  summarise(
    ymin = min(value),
    ymax = max(value),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    range = ymax - ymin,
    mid = (ymin + ymax) / 2
  ) 

```


The 2026 Men's World Cup will feature [a record number of players over age 40 — nearly as many as all prior World Cups combined](https://www.fifa.com/en/tournaments/mens/worldcup/canadamexicousa2026/articles/eight-players-aged-40-or-over).

And just below 40 years old, [players like the 38 year old Lionel Messi are also drawing attention for their staying power.](https://www.bbc.com/sport/articles/c74y97k5jqpo) 

Is it just a bias in attention, as Ronaldo and Messi happen to be (likely) coming to the end of their unusually long careers at the same tournament? Or are we really seeing an increase in older World Cup players?

**Are men's World Cup squads getting older, and is there an increase in longevity?** 

::: {style="margin-left: 2em;"}
This can be broken into two different questions, and I'm primarily interested in the second one:\
(1) Men's World Cup squads getting older could be examined with trends over time in central summaries likes means or medians.\
(2) "Longevity" as I am imagining it is the more interesting aspect, but a bit more complicated to conceptualize. To focus on the oldest players, I don't want an arbitrary cutoff like 40 and just counting players above that threshold; I also don't want to focus on a singular outlier of the oldest player at each tournament. I will use upper percentiles (or in statistics: quantiles), similar to how economic tracking of income over time might focus on the changing value of income of the upper 5% (aka the .95 quantile or 95th percentile) or upper 1% (aka the .99 quantile or 99th percentile).^[I will prefer to to use the slightly-more-colloquial term "percentile" over "quantile" in discussions and visuals, just to be a bit more broadly understood.]\
\
We will further clarify these ideas of longevity (and it's distinction from just mean/median getting older) when we get into analysis techniques.^[As my ability to conceptualize the question was improved by learning new analysis techniques!]

:::

I will use a dataset all players named to World Cup squads from the 1930-2022 World Cups from the [World Cup database](https://www.worldcups.ai/) (© 2026 Joshua C. Fjelstudl, Ph.D., [CC-BY-SA 4.0 license](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/legalcode)). In addition, I added the 2026 players from web scrapping [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_FIFA_World_Cup_squads). More [Data Details](#sec-data-details) are further below in the Appendix, and are fully documented on the [separate github repository for this project](https://github.com/LindsayRankin/mens-world-cup-age). 

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Assumptions about player data

I am considering any player named to a squad as a World Cup player (that is, not distinguishing playing time or excluding unused squad members), and calculating their age at each World Cup from the start date of that tournament. 

Conceptually I am interested in topics about training, recovery, and general wellness leading to [sustained high performance into older ages](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/06/magazine/pro-athletes-longevity-secrets-age.html). That's quite a complicated question I can't really address with this data. Here we are just trying to first establish if there really are any signs of increasing player longevity. But I want to make explicit the following assumption:\
**I am broadly imagining the players selected for each squad as the best available for that team/country. That is, a player is on a squad because they are high performing, and therefore if they are older they would represent the kind of high performing longevity I am interested in.**\

There could be other forces at work in how managers select players for a squad (e.g., nostalgia for formerly great players that fans or teammates want to stay on the squad). It may not be anything about players changing, but just the willingness of managers to select older players. While I would not totally discount these possibilities, winning should be the primary motivation of all managers and that may ultimately tip the scales over these other considerations, so I would like to at least talk about the data with the assumption that players are the best possible selections. 

In addition, players have to play as a team, and different managers may have different philosophies and balances in constructing a team. Teams are also drawn from the men in a country (leaving aside some complications of players with multiple potential eligibility, where a player must ultimately make a single, final commitment), and different countries may also have different demographic factors (e.g., differences in generation sizes) and football development factors (e.g., if there were particular periods of time they began investing more into development). 

We can somewhat improve our representation of at least some of these team-level considerations by representing players as being clustered within squads, which will change standard error calculations and therefore confidence intervals. When available to (relatively easily) implement, clustering by squad within a year will be ideal; but given the fun and exploratory nature of this project, I will note that at times this becomes overly burdensome and I made a choice to give up some accuracy/precision for keeping the scope of this project manageable.

Finally, as the tournament has expanded to more teams over time, it's possible that these newer teams (who would have been outside of qualification prior to expansions) may differ in how they select players, and those team differences may contribute to differences in players over time. Some follow up analyses will attempt to address some of these alternative explanations. 

:::


# World Cups 1930-2026 

Although there is great variability in individual player ages (calculated from the start date of each tournament), a smoothed trend line of age has been generally increasing over time (with the notable exception of a dip in the decades immediately following World War II). 

I had decided (a priori / before looking at this data) to focus my analysis to the time periods decades after the end of World War II. In addition to suspending the World Cup during the 1940's, I would expect a number of lingering effects on potential players, in particular a limited pool of older players in the decades to follow. 

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## World War II potential effects on player age

Specifically, there would have been greater injury and mortality among military-aged men in countries involved in the war, so it seems reasonable to suspect that would have left fewer potential best players in their 20's-40's for the next couple decades when World Cup tournaments resumed. 

It may also be reasonable to suspect other influences, such as those military-aged generations being able to devote less time and energy to sports during their developmental years compared to later generations who were young children during the war or born after it. 

Both of these aspects would be external shocks that favored youth in the decades to follow, and then after that time period it could have made it look like squads were getting older just as a correction to these influences. 

While I am not testing any *why* about age increasing, as noted above I am conceptually more interested in a general increase in longevity that [could *arguably* be due to more interesting (to me) aspects like training, recovery, and wellness,](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/06/magazine/pro-athletes-longevity-secrets-age.html) rather than attributable to an external shock like war. So I would like to avoid analyses including these immediate post-war years that could have such an easy alternative explanation. 
:::


```{r}
#| output: true
#| out-width: "100%"

#----------------------------------- 
# Main overall age graph
#----------------------------------- 
# # Label some individual players
  # First over 40 and oldest ever
labels_oldest <- dfsquads_1930_2026 %>%
  filter(year < 2026, age > 40,
         family_name %in% c("Yashin", "El Hadary"))

# Overall main player age graph
dfsquads_1930_2026 %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = age)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(color = age > 40),
              shape = 21, fill = NA, # just outlines, no fill
              height = 0, width = .8, alpha=.3) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "FALSE" = palette_green,
      "TRUE"  = palette_red
    ),
    # name = "Age > 40"
    guide = "none"
  ) + 
  geom_text_repel(
    data = labels_oldest,
    aes(label = paste0(family_name, ", ", team_name, " ", year," (Age ", round(age, 1), ")")),
    size = 2.5,
    # Placement above, more space
    direction = "y",     # only move labels vertically
    nudge_y = 1,         # start 1 unit above the point
    vjust = 0,           # text extends upward from the anchor
    # The label to data connector
    segment.color = "grey",
    segment.size = 0.5,
    segment.alpha = 1,
    min.segment.length = 0
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 40,
    color = palette_red,
    linewidth = .5,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_smooth(se=FALSE, color = palette_blue) + 
  # To only show actual years in the data
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = sort(unique(dfsquads_1930_2026$year)), 
    guide = guide_axis(angle = 45), 
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.02)) # extra space on the right
  ) +
  labs(title = "Men's World Cup (1930-2026) Player Ages",
       subtitle = "Players 40+ Years Old (red)",
       x = "Year", y = "Player Age (Years)") + 
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(# only break years for vertical lines
    panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank())
```

In terms of the article/Instagram representation of longevity of 40+ year old players, the first appeared in 1970 (Lev Yashin was an unused squad member for the Soviet Union), the oldest in 2018 (Egypt's Essam El-Hadary at over 45 years), but the number of players at or even near 40 seems to have increased in recent years. There were seven men 40+ at the start of the 2026 tournament — compared to just nine total in all prior years.^[Note a slight difference in definition compared to the FIFA's article and Instagram post: Uruguay's Fernando Muslera turned 40 during the tournament — see the "Age at 16 June 2026" notation in the Instagram post. I calculated age for players at each tournament from each tournament start date, so Muslera's age in my data would be 39.98631. In addition, I looked at all players named to a squads, while the [FIFA article](https://www.fifa.com/en/tournaments/mens/worldcup/canadamexicousa2026/articles/eight-players-aged-40-or-over) focused only on those who saw playing time and therefore excluded unused squad members.] 

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Players 40+ years old in the 2026 tournament
Based on age at the start date of the tournament.

```{r}
dfsquads_1930_2026 %>%
  filter(age >=40, year == 2026) %>%
  arrange(desc(age)) %>%
  mutate(Name = paste0(ifelse(is.na(given_name),
                              "", # no given_name Vozinha
                              given_name),
                       " ", family_name),
         Age = round(age, 1)) %>% # use fmt_number
  select(Name,
         Team = team_name,
         Position = squad_position_name,
         Age) %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = Age,
    decimals = 1
  ) %>%
  tab_header(title = "2026 World Cup Players 40+ Years Old") %>% 
  tab_options(table.align = "left")
```

::: 

But as discussed, drawing a line right at 40 also seem a bit arbitrary — and we can see that recent years seem to have many more older players just below this threshold (potentially even when taking into account the greater number of players per tournaments in more recent years). 


# Expansion Era (1982-2026)

I will limit my analysis to World Cup tournaments from 1982 until 2026. The 1982 World Cup could be referred to a the beginning of an "expansion era" of the tournament, as it increased from 16 to 24 teams. This format change is far enough out from the shadow of WWII to hopefully minimize those direct influences (someone born at the end of WWII in 1944 would be 38 years old by the 1982 tournament), as well as providing a larger sample size of players, so it thus serves as a good conceptual cut point. 


```{r}
#| include: false

#----------------------------------- 
############ Sample sizes 
#----------------------------------- 
# Table display of sample sizes 
  # For seeing / reporting numbers in text
dfsquads %>% 
  group_by(year, team_code) %>% 
  summarize(`Players per Team` = n()) %>% 
  group_by(year) %>% 
  summarize(`Total Teams` = n(),
            `Total Players` = sum(`Players per Team`)) %>% 
  rename(Year = year) # %>% filter(Year %in% c(1982, 2026))

```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Sample size details

Specifically, the tournament expanded in 1982 to 26 teams and a total of 526 players (unusually, a couple of the 22 squad spots went unused that year, but the total number of players was 528 for the next three tournaments).\ 
In the years since, the tournament experienced additional expansions in the number of teams and a upticks in squad size (from 22 to 23 and eventually 26), reaching 1248 players on 48 teams in 2026. 

```{r}
#| output: true
#| out-width: "100%"

#----------------------------------- 
########## Sample size graphs - teams and players
#----------------------------------- 
########## Player and Teams Counts
### Putting on to one graph
# Create both summaries

    .groups = "drop"

# Scaling factor

ggplot(plot_sample_df, aes(x = year)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = total_players, color = "Players"), linewidth = 1) +

    )
  ) +

    values = c("Players" = palette_green, "Teams" = palette_red),

  ) +
   # Vertical reference lines

        axis.text.y = element_text(color = palette_green),
```

# World Cups 1982-2026: Are men's World Cup squads getting older? 

Age distributions in tournament years had small positive skews (all <= .43), and means and medians were generally quite similar.

::: 

Using a linear regression fit line during the expansion era, predicted mean player age was increasing by .07 years or 25 days at each tournament since 1982.^[The coefficient .0174 is the change in age per year. Tournaments are every four years, and there are 365.25 days in each year: .0174 \* 4 years/tournament = .07 years increase per tournament and .0174 \* 4 years/tournament \* 365.25 days/year = 25.36 days increase per tournament. Note that years were calculated as years since 1982 to make the intercept interpretable as the predicted mean age in 1982.] Collectively, this shows an increase from an average predicted age of 27.01 in 1982 to 27.78 in 2026, a bit over 3/4ths of a year increase - not a massive increase, but a non-trivial cumulative result that players are getting a bit older. 

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

But this increase in mean age cannot address the second and more interesting question about changes in longevity. 

For this, we turn to quantile regression. 

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## From percentile explorations to quantile regression

Quantile regression is new to me, so this was a learning experience! 

I was initially hitting a bit of a roadblock: 

I had visually explored trends in percentile values calculated per year. I had looked at lower percentiles to confirm that changes in mean age were not being driven by just avoiding selecting youth; if anything, lower percentiles were flat or trending slightly downwards, that is selecting even younger players. So I felt confident in saying that increases in mean age were not just driven by avoiding youth.

```{r}
#| output: true
#| out-width: "100%"

# YOUNGER summary stats
stats_to_plot <- c("Min", "01st", "05th", "10th", "15th", "20th")


# For each particular set of graphs, set these limits so percentile graphs have same range
limits_df_stats_to_plot <- bind_rows(
  # Exclude EXCEPTIONS Min, Max, then bind those
  limits_df %>%
    filter(name %in% setdiff(stats_to_plot, c(# "Mean", "Median", 
      "Min", "Max"))) %>% 
    mutate(
      ymin_graph = mid - max(range) / 2,
      ymax_graph = mid + max(range) / 2
    ),
  # bind the EXCEPTION

             name %in% stats_to_plot) %>%

  ) %>% 
  # all rows, now arrange
    mutate(name = factor(name, levels = stats_to_plot)) %>%

# Build one scale per facet
y_scales <- purrr::map2(

)

### Plotting selected stats_to_plot
```

But beyond these graphs and calculating changes at the end points, I was initially stumped as to how to further represent these changes, particularly how to summarize them into statistics. And how to extend it to considerations of other variables, like a player's position. I wanted something like a linear regression slope, but for some kind of longevity measure rather than a mean. 🤔

Enter [quantile regression, particularly as outlined by Roger Koenker](http://www.econ.uiuc.edu/~roger/research/rq/QRJEP.pdf), and implemented in his [quantreg package in R](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/quantreg/index.html). This seemed like [a great set of approaches](https://rkoenker.github.io/www/roger/research/rq/rq.html) for this question.

So this is an exploration and learning experience. I am a bit unsure (as I am stepping into new analyses with somewhat complicated clustered data and later exploring some interaction effects) or knowingly doing not-quite-ideal analyses (particularly with respect to some limitations for standard error calculations / analyses that cannot represent the clustered data without creating custom code that will be computationally intense, as discussed below), but I want to float some ideas. I'm also going to take more of an explaining/teaching tone to parts of this as I am teaching myself.

::: 

# World Cups 1982-2026: Are men's World Cup squads increasing in longevity? Quantile regression approach

With quantile regression, instead of representing the slope of change in mean age over time, we can consider the change in age over time of any particular quantile or percentile. 

First, it's worth noting that a quantile regression prediction of the median (aka the 50th percentile or .50 quantile) does not really conceptually differ from our linear regression mean prediction — by either measure, central age is increasing a bit over time, and in very similar ways. 

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Mean vs median prediction lines

You didn't believe me? So similar! 😂

```{r}
#| output: true
#| out-width: "100%"

dfsquads %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = age, 
             )) +
  geom_jitter(color = palette_green,
              shape = 21, fill = NA,
              height = 0, width = .8, alpha=.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = palette_red, 
              linetype = "dashed",
              se = FALSE
              ) +
  geom_quantile(quantiles = .5, color = palette_blue,
                alpha = .8, # linetype = "twodash", 
                linewidth = 1
                ) +
  # To only show actual years in the data
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = sort(unique(dfsquads$year)), 
    guide = guide_axis(angle = 45), 
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, # 0.02)) # extra space on the right
                                .12)) # extra room for labels
  ) +
  labs(title = "Men's World Cup (1982-2026) Player Ages",
       subtitle = "Linear regression mean fit line (red) and quantile regression median fit line (blue)",
       x = "Year", y = "Player Age (Years)") + 
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none")
```
::: 

But we want to examine the slopes over time of different quantiles or percentiles of the age. Given this new quantile regression framework, we can actually further refine or clarify our research questions and separate our 'longevity increasing' second question into two components: 

::: {style="margin-left: 2em;"}
1. **Location shift of longevity**: The slope of change in age over time for the 95th or 99th percentile can represent that the older players are getting older.\
\
But this may be a part of an overall "location shift" of just getting older where the center of age is also increasing (mean/median ages are going up, as are the oldest ages) consistent with the first overall research question of "squads getting older"; it could be that the whole distribution of age shifts in its location, so players at any point (median, 95th or 99th percentiles) are all getting older over time. Thus, we need to distinguish a second aspect:

2. **Shape shift of longevity**: Difference of the slopes of age over time of these upper percentiles compared to or relative to changes for the rest of the distribution would tell us that there is a change in the shape of the distribution of age. If the slope of age over time for the 95th percentile of age is greater than the slope of age over time at the median, than it is indicating that small number of players are getting increasingly or relatively older above and beyond any possible overall age increases elsewhere in the distribution. In terms of the shape of the distribution of age, it's not about (just) a location shift but (also) a shape shift with the upper tail of the distribution stretching out.  
:::


To consider using quantile regression, a first check can be if slopes at different quantiles do seem to differ. In addition to clustering players by their squads (specifically the particular team by year), we will use quantreg summary.rq functions to estimate standard errors empirically through bootstrapping. 

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Do we need quantile regression?

If a quantile regression shows us that we have no differences in the slopes of age over time for any particular percentile of age, then there is very little need to continue to modeling each of these other percentiles separately. But if we see different slopes for the upper percentiles compared to the median, this may hint at a "shape shift of longevity" possibility that there is a minority of the very oldest players outlasting prior age norms, and it is worth investigating these quantile regression results further. 
:::


As in the linear regression, the slopes represent the predicted change for each year since 1982.^[In this initial graph the slopes are per year simply because we can lean on functions built for quantreg and not need customization. But in later visualizations we will represent slopes by multiplying this coefficient by 4 years so that it will represent the change in age expected per World Cup.] We can find the coefficients for the fit lines across all percentiles (that is, quantiles from .04 to .99 by .05 increments).^[In terms of pure speed/burning up my local computer memory, I found by .01 problematically slow; the quantreg plot.rq function needs evenly spaced intervals for the plot, and by using .04 to .99 I will get an estimate for .94 and .99 which is close enough for an initial look to my desired 95th and 99th percentile.]  In the plot below, the different quantiles are represented along the x axis, and the values of slope (in units per year) for each of those quantile regressions is shown on the y axis and represented with the black dots and dashed line (and grey confidence intervals); the red represents the coefficients and confidence interval from the linear regression for comparison.

We see that the slope of age over time does differ by quantiles of age (the line of slopes by quantiles is not flat), and does differ from the mean prediction of a linear regression slope (it is outside the red bounds). 


```{r}
#| label: fit-model-sum_quantreg_seqby05_bootSEcluster
#| eval: false

# speed / efficiency:
  # due to processing time during local development: 
  # save the model locally, then in a separate code chunk just load it
  # Only manually rerun this chunk to resave the model if there are changes to the data or this 
    # simply because all these bootstraps take so long

# Fuller values of tau to actually represent the .95 and .99 might be ideal
  # so something like tau = seq(.01, .99, by = .01)
  # BUT this plot.rq needs/assumes equal spaced taus
  # and the .01 increment along that full scale takes way too long and often crashes my local machine (July 2026 before upgrade)
  # I will use seq(.04, .99, by = .05), which will including .94 and .99
quantreg_seqby05 <- rq(age ~ Years.Since.1982, data = dfsquads, 
                       tau = seq(.04, .99, by = .05))

set.seed(123)
sum_quantreg_seqby05_bootSEcluster <- 
  summary(quantreg_seqby05,
          se = "boot", 
          cluster = dfsquads$team_year_cluster,                                       
          R = num_boot_sim)

saveRDS(sum_quantreg_seqby05_bootSEcluster,
        file = "sum_quantreg_seqby05_bootSEcluster.rds")

```

```{r}
#| output: true
#| out-width: "100%"

sum_quantreg_seqby05_bootSEcluster <- readRDS("sum_quantreg_seqby05_bootSEcluster.rds")

plot(sum_quantreg_seqby05_bootSEcluster,
     parm = "Years.Since.1982") # don't shown intercept, just slope

```


::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Further details on interpreting the graph

Specifically, at a quantile around .5 (the median) the slope does not differ from the linear regression mean predictions (represented by the red lines) because it's is well within those red bounds. However, the lowest quantiles are differing from these predictions, and generally do not differ from zero (the horizontal black line) — indicating that the ages among the youngest players selected are not changing at each World Cup. But of primary interest is the upper quantiles that show greater slopes, indicating that the oldest players are not only getting older consistent with a "location shift of longevity" like at the mean and median, but that upper minority of the oldest players may be getting older at an even greater rate than other parts of the distribution of age, consistent with the possibility of a "shape shift of longevity".
::: 

Therefore, a linear regression of the mean or a quantile regression of the median slope do not represent the changes in age over time for the more extreme ages and could obscure these differences, and we need to use quantile regression to represent these upper percentiles of interest.

To make it more concrete, we can graph the equations of some of the quantile regression lines on the original data (converting to changes in age per World Cup tournament "/WC", that is every four years) to more clearly see that both the 95th and 99th percentiles demonstrate not only positive slopes for a "location shift of longevity", but they may have even steeper slopes and stretching the upper part of the distribution faster than the upward trajectory of the rest of the distribution, consistent with the possibility of a "shape shift of longevity". 

```{r}
#| label: quantreg_tauval
#| output: true
#| out-width: "100%"

tauval <- c(.05, .5, .95, .99)
taulab <- c("05th", "50th", "95th", "99th")
tau_key <- tibble(tau = tauval, tau_label = taulab)

quantreg_tauval <- rq(age ~ Years.Since.1982, data = dfsquads, tau = tauval)

# With only year as predictor, it will be repetitive in the data
  # Match to year, grab distinct
pred_tauval <- data.frame(dfsquads %>% select(year), 
                          quantreg_tauval$fitted.values) %>% 
  distinct() 

colnames(pred_tauval) <- c("year", taulab)

# Pivot longer for graphing
pred_tauval <- pred_tauval %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    -year, 
    names_to = "Percentile", 
    values_to = "age",
  ) %>% 
  arrange(year, Percentile)

# Labels for lines 
line_labels <- pred_tauval %>%
  group_by(Percentile) %>%
  slice_max(year, n = 1) %>%
  ungroup()

# Label of slopes; year and age determine placement on graph
  # can get from coefficents, but more complicated; just compute from predicted
slope_labels <-
  pred_tauval %>%
  group_by(Percentile) %>%
  summarize(
    slope_per_wc = ((age[year == 2026] - age[year == 1982]) / 44) * 4,
    age = age[year == 2006],   # for graph placement
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    year = 2006,               # for graph placement
    label = sprintf("%+.3f/WC", slope_per_wc)
  )

# Place percentiles on top of: 
# Overall main player age graph
  # Labels of slopes aren't matching color... but this graph is probably too busy
dfsquads %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = age, 
             color = Percentile # not in dfsquads, but matches labels to color
             )) +
  geom_jitter(color = "grey",# palette_green,
              shape = 21, fill = NA,
              height = 0, width = .8, alpha=.3) +
  geom_line(data = pred_tauval, 
            mapping = aes(x = year, y = age, color = Percentile)) + 
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") + 
  # Labels by lines instead of legend
  geom_text(
    data = line_labels,
    aes(label = Percentile),
    size = 3.5,
    hjust = -0.1,
    vjust = 0.5,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  # Slopes
  geom_label(
    data = slope_labels,
    aes(label = label),
    fill = scales::alpha("white", .75),
    #color = "black",
    size = 3.5,
    linewidth = 0, # label.size = 0,
    label.padding = unit(.08, "lines"),
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  # To only show actual years in the data
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = sort(unique(dfsquads$year)), 
    guide = guide_axis(angle = 45), 
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, # 0.02)) # extra space on the right
                                .12)) # extra room for labels
  ) +
  labs(title = "Men's World Cup (1982-2026) Player Ages",
       subtitle = "Quantile Regression Fit Lines at Selected Percentiles",
       caption = "Note: Slopes represent change in age per World Cup (every 4 years) for each percentile",
       x = "Year", y = "Player Age (Years)") + 
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none")

```
Looking at the significance testing of each of these slopes seperately, we can confirm the "location shift of longevity": There is a significant increase in age over time at the 95th and 99th percentiles, but also at the median or 50th percentile. 

```{r}
#| label: fit-model-sum_all_tau
#| eval: false

# speed / efficiency:
  # due to processing time during local development: 
  # save the model locally, then in a separate code chunk just load it
  # Only manually rerun this chunk to resave the model if there are changes to the data or this 
    # simply because all these bootstraps take so long

### calculations done here, with SE with bootstrapping and clustering
  # can be slow, depending on num_boot_sim (set to 200 for testing; 600+ final)
set.seed(123)
sum_all_tau <- summary(
  quantreg_tauval,
  se = "boot", 
  covariance = TRUE,      # <- needed to get $B (bootstrap draws) alongside coefficients for calculating predicted values
  cluster = dfsquads$team_year_cluster, 
  R = num_boot_sim
)
# sum_all_tau is a list, one element per tau, in the same order as tauval

saveRDS(sum_all_tau,
        file = "sum_all_tau.rds")


```


```{r}
#| label: sum_all_tau
#| output: true
#| out-width: "100%"

# saved for efficiency, eval: false on its creation, not rendered and must be recreated manually
sum_all_tau <- readRDS("sum_all_tau.rds")


# # These must match how this model was run
  # Should when code is run in order
# tauval <- c(.05, .5, .95, .99)
# taulab <- c("05th", "50th", "95th", "99th")
# tau_key <- tibble(tau = tauval, tau_label = taulab)

# Table of slopes for significance and CIs and predicted values
  # Will be reused later for core vs non-core team tables
make_table_slopeCIpred <- function(which_team = "All", 
                                   # "Core", #"Non Core",
                                   which_model = sum_all_tau,
                                   # sum_coreteam_tau, # sum_noncoreteam_tau
                                   which_tauval = tauval,
                                   which_tau_key = tau_key){
  # Table title depending on team core vs non core or original analysis
  if (which_team %in% c("Core", "Non-Core", "Non Core")) {
    table_title <- paste0("Player Age by Percentile, ", which_team, " Teams")
  } else {
    table_title <- "Player Age by Percentile"
  }
  
  
  # Calculations
  slopes_df <- map2_dfr(which_model, which_tauval, function(s, tv) {
    cf <- s$coefficients
    age_change <- cf["Years.Since.1982", "Value"] * 4
    se_change  <- cf["Years.Since.1982", "Std. Error"] * 4
    tibble(
      tau            = tv,
      AgeChangePerWC = age_change,
      SEPerWC        = se_change,
      lower.CL.PerWC = age_change - qnorm(.975) * se_change,
      upper.CL.PerWC = age_change + qnorm(.975) * se_change,
      p.value        = cf["Years.Since.1982", "Pr(>|t|)"]
    )
  }) %>% 
    left_join(which_tau_key, by = "tau")
  
  pred_df <- map2_dfr(which_model, which_tauval, function(s, tv) {
    cf <- s$coefficients
    B  <- s$B
    colnames(B) <- rownames(cf)   # B has no dimnames by default; columns are in the same order as cf's rows
    
    map_dfr(c(`1982` = 0, `2026` = 44), function(x) {
      pred      <- cf["(Intercept)", "Value"] + cf["Years.Since.1982", "Value"] * x
      boot_pred <- B[, "(Intercept)"] + B[, "Years.Since.1982"] * x
      # more direct/empirical/non-covariance-formula way of calculating SE of predicted values 
      se_pred   <- sd(boot_pred)
      tibble(
        emmean   = pred,
        SE       = se_pred,
        lower.CL = pred - qnorm(.975) * se_pred,
        upper.CL = pred + qnorm(.975) * se_pred
      )
    }, .id = "year_label") %>% 
      mutate(tau = tv)
  }) %>% 
    pivot_wider(
      id_cols     = tau,
      names_from  = year_label,
      values_from = c(emmean, SE, lower.CL, upper.CL),
      names_glue  = "{.value}_{year_label}"
    )
  
  
  combined_table <- slopes_df %>% 
    left_join(pred_df, by = "tau") %>% 
    select(tau_label, AgeChangePerWC, SEPerWC, lower.CL.PerWC, upper.CL.PerWC, p.value,
           emmean_1982, SE_1982, lower.CL_1982, upper.CL_1982,
           emmean_2026, SE_2026, lower.CL_2026, upper.CL_2026) %>% 
    arrange(match(tau_label, taulab))   # keep your original tau ordering, not alphabetical
  
  combined_table %>% 
    gt(rowname_col = "tau_label") %>% 
    fmt_number(
      columns = c(AgeChangePerWC, SEPerWC, lower.CL.PerWC, upper.CL.PerWC),
      decimals = 3
    ) %>% 
    fmt_number( # Age means just 1 decimal
      columns = c(emmean_1982, SE_1982, lower.CL_1982, upper.CL_1982,
                  emmean_2026, SE_2026, lower.CL_2026, upper.CL_2026),
      decimals = 1
    ) %>% 
    fmt(
      columns = p.value,
      fns = function(x) ifelse(x < .001, "<.001", sub("^0\\.", ".", sprintf("%.3f", x)))
    ) %>% 
    cols_merge(columns = c(lower.CL.PerWC, upper.CL.PerWC), pattern = "[{1}, {2}]") %>% 
    cols_merge(columns = c(lower.CL_1982, upper.CL_1982),   pattern = "[{1}, {2}]") %>% 
    cols_merge(columns = c(lower.CL_2026, upper.CL_2026),   pattern = "[{1}, {2}]") %>% 
    cols_label(
      AgeChangePerWC = "Age Δ /WC", SEPerWC = "SE", lower.CL.PerWC = "95% CI", p.value = "p",
      emmean_1982 = "Age", SE_1982 = "SE", lower.CL_1982 = "95% CI",
      emmean_2026 = "Age", SE_2026 = "SE", lower.CL_2026 = "95% CI"
    ) %>% 
    tab_spanner(label = "Slope (per WC cycle)", columns = c(AgeChangePerWC, SEPerWC, lower.CL.PerWC, p.value)) %>% 
    tab_spanner(label = "Predicted Age, 1982",  columns = c(emmean_1982, SE_1982, lower.CL_1982)) %>% 
    tab_spanner(label = "Predicted Age, 2026",  columns = c(emmean_2026, SE_2026, lower.CL_2026)) %>% 
    cols_align(align = "center", 
               columns = c(AgeChangePerWC, SEPerWC, lower.CL.PerWC, p.value,
                           emmean_1982, SE_1982, lower.CL_1982, emmean_2026, SE_2026, lower.CL_2026)) %>% 
    tab_style(style = cell_text(align = "left"), locations = cells_stub()) %>% 
    tab_header(title    = table_title,
               subtitle = paste0("Quantile regression slopes and predicted ages, with clustered bootstrapped SEs (", 
                                 num_boot_sim, " resamples)")
    ) %>% 
    tab_footnote(
      footnote = "Note: Predicted value SEs are empirically calculating from bootstrapped samples",
      locations = cells_column_labels(columns = c(SE_1982, SE_2026))
    ) %>% 
    tab_style(
      style = cell_text(align = "right"),
      locations = cells_footnotes()
    ) %>% 
    tab_options(table.align = "left")
  
}


make_table_slopeCIpred(which_team = "All", 
                       which_model = sum_all_tau)


```

To make it concrete, we can say that it predicts to a 2 year increase in the 95th percentile of age (from 32.9 to 34.9) during the 44 years of the expansion era of the tournament, and a 2.4 year increase in the 99th percentile of age (from 35.6 to 38.0).

To formally test the "shape shift of longevity", we would want to test the difference of the slopes at the upper percentiles compared to at the median. The quantreg package in R, however, does not have the ability to conduct these tests with bootstrapped standard errors that take into account clustering.^[This is just a current, known limitation of the quantreg package, as acknowledged in the anova.rq function help files.] I'll note that this could be custom built, but given the time to build and the challenges with the processing time/speed it would require to run such code compared to the intended scope of this project, I am going to skip this.^[Specifically, using summary.rq with clustering and bootstrapped SEs can already be a bit slow running on my local machine. While I did not fully build it out, some initial looks at the resampling and processing steps needed to implement this made it clear it would be very slow, and someone building this would really benefit from a greater understanding than I have of how best to program within R from a speed/efficiency perspective, or implement it using parallel processing.] 

Instead, I will use models with standard errors estimated *without* bootstrap resampling and *without* taking into account the clustering in calculating these slope differences to at least give some hints of whether we see differences, acknowledging the limitations with these very "rough SE-limitation comparisons".^[My standard errors will likely be too small, and therefore my significance testing p-values will be biased downwards increasing the risk of Type I errors.]

I compared the slopes at the median, 95th, and 99th percentiles (using these "rough SE-limitation comparisons"), and there are overall differences. Using follow up pairwise comparisons (with the Holm correction for multiple comparisons), we can see that both the 95th percentile and 99th percentile slopes are significantly larger than the median, but do not differ from each other. 

```{r}

taus_to_compare <- c(.5, .95, .99)
tau_pairs <- combn(taus_to_compare, 2, simplify = FALSE)

# # Not taking into account clustered SEs or using bootstrapped SEs
# anova(rq(age ~ Years.Since.1982, 
#          data = dfsquads, 
#          tau = taus_to_compare), 
#       test = "Wald")

pairwise_wald <- map_dfr(tau_pairs, function(p) {
  fit_pair <- rq(age ~ Years.Since.1982, data = dfsquads, tau = p)
  a   <- anova(fit_pair, test = "Wald")   # se = "nid" by default -- fast, not bootstrapped
  tab <- a$table
  tibble(
    tau_lower = p[1],
    tau_upper = p[2],
    F_value   = tab[, ncol(tab) - 1],
    p_value   = tab[, ncol(tab)]
  )
}) %>% 
  mutate(p_adj = p.adjust(p_value, method = "holm"))  # correcting for testing 3 pairs


# Table 
pairwise_wald %>% 
  mutate(Comparison = paste0("\u03c4=", sprintf("%.2f", tau_lower), 
                              " vs \u03c4=", sprintf("%.2f", tau_upper))) %>% 
  select(Comparison, F_value, p_value, p_adj) %>% 
  gt(rowname_col = "Comparison") %>% 
  fmt_number(
    columns = F_value,
    decimals = 3
  ) %>% 
  fmt(
    columns = c(p_value, p_adj),
    fns = function(x) {
      ifelse(x < .001, 
             "<.001", 
             sub("^0\\.", ".", sprintf("%.3f", x)))
    }
  ) %>% 
  cols_label(
    F_value = "F",
    p_value = "p (raw)",
    p_adj   = "p (Holm-adjusted)"
  ) %>% 
  cols_align(align = "center", columns = c(F_value, p_value, p_adj)) %>% 
  tab_style(style = cell_text(align = "left"), locations = cells_stub()) %>% 
  tab_header(
    title    = "Pairwise Comparisons of Slopes Across Quantiles",
    subtitle = "Wald tests, analytic (nid) SEs \u2014 not bootstrapped or cluster-adjusted"
  ) %>% 
  tab_options(table.align = "left")
```

We have support for the "shape shift of longevity" that oldest players are getting increasingly older, there is a stretching of the tail of the distribution (with the caveats of the "rough SE-limitation comparisons"). 

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Further visualzing the shape shift of longevity

We can visualize this by considering the changing distribution of age over time. The upper tail (as seen in those green and purple sections of the distribution) is stretching out and moving further to the right than the shifts of the median.

```{r}
#| label: age-dist-fn


# function for animated histogram of age distribution
  # ideal for Median and 95th percentile; 99th can be squeezed on

anim_age_dist_fn <- function(
  # Which position(s) to graph  
  position_choice = c("Goal keeper", "Defender", "Midfielder", "Forward"), 
      # Or single selections: 
        # position_choice = "Goal keeper"
        # position_choice = "Defender"
        # position_choice = "Midfielder"
        # position_choice = "Forward"
  stats_to_graph = c("Median", "95th"),
    # Or: 
      # stats_to_graph = c("Median", "95th", "99th"),
  # Start year(s) for comparison; select two complementary values and labels
  start_comp = 1982,
  start_comp_lab = as.character(start_comp),
    # Or:
      # start_comp = c(1982, 1986),
      # start_comp_lab = "1982-1986",
      # start_comp = c(1982, 1986, 1990),
      # start_comp_lab = "1982-1990",
  # Nudging up/down placement of distance year labels of each horizontal distance line 
  y_dist_top = .11,
  y_dist_bottom = .06,
  # 95th and 99th will otherwise overlap, custom moving
  nudge_down_99th = .003
    ) {
  
  # Data for this position (or all)
  df_plot <- dfsquads %>%
    filter(squad_position_name %in% position_choice) 
  
  # Graphing details 
  percentile_specs <-
  tibble(
    Percentile = c("Median", "95th", "99th"),
    word_labs = c("Median", "95th Percentile", "99th Percentile"),
    label_start_stat = paste0(start_comp_lab, " ", word_labs), 
    hjust = c(1, 0, 0),
    y_label_start_stat = case_when(
      Percentile %in% c("Median", "95th") ~ Inf,
      Percentile == "99th" ~ (y_dist_bottom - (nudge_down_99th*.3)) #label below 95ths
    )
  ) %>% 
    filter(Percentile %in% stats_to_graph)
  
  ### Lines and Labels 
  # To draw quantile lines
  quantiles <-
    df_plot %>%
    group_by(year) %>%
    summarize(
      Median = quantile(age,.5),
      `95th` = quantile(age,.95),
      `99th` = quantile(age,.99) 
    ) %>%
    pivot_longer(
      -year,
      names_to="Percentile",
      values_to="age"
    ) %>% 
    filter(Percentile %in% stats_to_graph) %>% 
    mutate(Percentile = factor(Percentile, # order
                               levels = stats_to_graph))
  
  # Start year or 80's average or first three tournament average
    # for labels and dashed lines
  quantiles_start_labels <-
    df_plot %>%
    filter(year %in% start_comp) %>%
    summarize(
      Median = quantile(age,.5),
      `95th`  = quantile(age,.95),
      `99th` = quantile(age,.99) 
    ) %>%
    pivot_longer(
      cols = everything(),
      names_to="Percentile",
      values_to="age"
    ) %>% 
    filter(Percentile %in% stats_to_graph) %>% 
    mutate(Percentile = factor(Percentile, # order
                               levels = stats_to_graph)) %>% 
    left_join(percentile_specs,
              by = "Percentile")
  
  
  # To draw horizontal line of distance changes 
    # from dashed start year stat line to current year stat line
    # exclude whatever years are included in start comparison
  history_dist <-
    quantiles %>%
    filter(!year %in% start_comp) %>% 
    bind_rows(
      quantiles_start_labels %>%
        select(Percentile, age) %>% 
        mutate(year = 1)
    ) %>%
    arrange(Percentile, year) %>%
    group_by(Percentile) %>%
    mutate(
      x0 = first(age),
      y = case_when(
        # placement of each year going down to keep them all on the graph
          # 99th has to be custom/odd to not overlap with 95th
        Percentile == "Median" ~ seq(y_dist_top, y_dist_bottom, length.out = n()),
        Percentile == "95th"   ~ seq(y_dist_top, y_dist_bottom, length.out = n()),
        Percentile == "99th"   ~ seq(y_dist_bottom - (2*nudge_down_99th), # shift down start
                                     ((y_dist_bottom - (2*nudge_down_99th)) - (y_dist_top-y_dist_bottom)),
                                     length.out = n())
      )
    ) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    filter(!year %in% c(1, 1982))
  
  
  ### Graph
    # year is implemented in transition_states, like a facet 
  anim_plot_fn <- 
    df_plot %>% 
    ggplot(aes(age)) + 
    # Density of current year, layer 1
    geom_density(
      fill = palette_green,
      alpha = .8,
      linewidth = 1
    ) +
    # Dashed line of current year quantile, layer 2
    geom_vline(
      data = quantiles,
      aes(xintercept = age,
          color = Percentile),
      linewidth = 1
    ) +
    ### Early years for comparison
    # Dashed line for early years
    geom_vline(
      data = quantiles_start_labels,
      aes(xintercept = age,
          color = Percentile),
      linewidth = 1,
      linetype = "dashed",
      alpha = .5
    ) +
    # Label of early years(s) stat
    geom_label(data = quantiles_start_labels,
               aes(x = age, y = y_label_start_stat,
                   label = label_start_stat, 
                   color = Percentile,
                   hjust = hjust
                   ),
               fill = "white",
               label.padding = unit(0, "lines"),
               linewidth = NA, # no box outline
               vjust = 1.7,
               size = 3.5) + 
    # Colors from "Set1"
    scale_color_manual(
      values = c(
        "Median" = palette_red,
        "95th" = palette_blue,
        "99th" = palette_purple
      )
    ) +
    ### Current years vs early year(s)
    # Drawing horizontal line to compare each stat to early years
    geom_segment(
      data = history_dist,
      aes(
        x = x0,
        xend = age,
        y = y,
        yend = y,
        color = Percentile
      ),
      linewidth = 1.2
    ) + 
    # Text of current year for comparing each stat to early years
    geom_label( 
      data = history_dist,
      aes(
        x = age + .1, # Just a bit of space
        y = y,
        label = year,
        color = Percentile
      ),
      fill = "white",
      label.padding = unit(0, "lines"),
      linewidth = NA, # no box outline around year
      hjust = 0,
      size = 3.5
    ) +
    # keep horizontal distance as it goes through years
    shadow_mark(
      past = TRUE,
      future = FALSE,
      alpha = .8,
      exclude_layer = c(1,2) #geom_* layers by count
    ) +
    transition_states(
      year,
      transition_length = 1,
      state_length = 5,
      wrap = FALSE # integrate into blog so reader can press play
    ) +
    labs(
      title = ifelse(length(position_choice) > 1,
                     yes = paste0("{closest_state} Distribution of Player Ages"),
                     no = paste0("{closest_state} Distribution of Player Ages for ",
                                 str_to_title(position_choice), "s")
      ),
      subtitle = "Changes by Year vs 1982 (dashed)",
      x = "Player Age (Years)", y = "" 
    ) +
    coord_cartesian(
      xlim = c(17, 46) # range in dfsquads
    ) + 
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(legend.position = "none",
          axis.text.y = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), 
          panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank()
    ) 
  
  return(anim_plot_fn)
}

```

We could also visualize this with a bit on animation.^[The image quality and resolution aspects are not ideal here, but I wanted to include this rough draft as it helped me to make the ideas of shape shift more concrete.] We can keep a constant marker of the starting point (1982 as a dashed line) as our comparison for the median, 95th percentile, and 99th percentile, and then observe the new position of each of those stats over time, and keep a trace of these shifts by drawing a horizontal distance line to the new position at each year versus the 1982 starting point. As can be seen, there is location shift — ages are increasing a bit at the median, 95th percentile, and 99th percentile in most years and therefore overall (i.e., if we imagine an 'average' shift of each). But there is also a shape shift: The upper tail of the distribution stretches out further to the right, and the increases in the 95th and 99th percentiles (again, visualized by the trace of each horizontal distance shift) not only tend to increase over time, they are also greater than the shift of the median. This is the shape shift of longevity. 

![](age_dist_allpositions.mp4){controls="1" loop="0"}



:::

But are these increases in longevity perhaps limited to or just driven by certain kinds of players? 

# Is it just goal keepers?

Although it was noted that a surprising number of older players on 2026 squads were field players (that is, the non-goal keeper positions of defenders, midfielders, and forwards), in general many of the oldest players at the 2026 and prior World Cups have been goalkeepers, as they ["typically face less physical wear and tear than outfield players, allowing many to extend their careers well into their late 30s and 40s."](https://sports.yahoo.com/articles/oldest-players-world-cup-where-150715142.html) Thus, it's reasonable to ask if it's just goal keepers driving these longevity trends. 

When we consider different position, we should be mindful that their sample sizes per tournament year do get quite small, particularly for goal keepers. Thus the 99th percentiles in particular may become quite unstable and should be interpreted with a bit of caution; I will focus more on the 95th percentile as our primary longevity metric, and even among goal keepers we should note it still represents very small numbers of players. 


::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Sample size by position details

No position group exceeded 200 before 1998, indicating that a 99th percentile represents fewer than the oldest two individuals. Further, prior to the 2026 tournament expansions, there were only between 69 and 99 goal keepers per tournament.

```{r}
#| output: true
#| out-width: "100%"

#----------------------------------- 
########## Sample size graph - players by position
#----------------------------------- 
dfsquads %>%
  group_by(year, squad_position_name) %>%
  summarise(
    total_players = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = total_players, color = squad_position_name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, alpha = .8) +
  geom_point(alpha = .8) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Total Players",
    limits = c(50, 450),
    breaks = seq(0, 450, by=50),
  ) + 
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1", 
                   name = "Position") + 
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = sort(unique(dfsquads$year)), # Only use actual years in data
    guide = guide_axis(angle = 45),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.02)) # extra space, equal each side
  ) +
  labs(title = "Men's World Cup Expansion Era (1982-2026)",
       subtitle = "Sample Sizes: Player Counts by Position",
       x = "Year") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        legend.direction = "horizontal",
        # horizontal line breaks
        panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "grey85", linewidth = 0.4),
        panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank(),
        # remove vertical line breaks
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
        )


```
:::

We can implement this with a time by position interaction, and focus on slope of time for each position.^[Conceptually the lower order term of time represents the effect for the position used as the reference group; we can relevel position in repeated models to extract these, but the coding shortcut is to use emmeans package to get each of these slopes. Also, one could also look at the interaction terms to test if the effect of time significantly *differed* for positions; however, given that I would expect each position to have similar direction of effects, just weaker or stronger, and given the small sample sizes by positions, such comparisons would be under-powered to test small differences. In other words, saying that goal keepers change in age over time at a particular percentile does not significantly differ from the change over time for another position is *not* particularly convincing when such comparisons are under-powered. For the current goal of assessing if just goal keepers are driving the longevity effects, I would prefer to focus on the slopes for each position separately and make conceptual arguments, rather than using a bunch of under-powered direct tests between positions.]

We see consistent patterns: Although goal keepers are older overall, all positions show "location shift of longevity" in the direction of ages of their upper percentiles increasing. And again, at least with respect to the raw values of the slopes those upper percentiles may be increasing at greater rates, potentially consistent with "shape shift of longevity" (with the exception of the particularly-concerningly-small-sample size of the 99th percentile for goal keepers, although their 95th percentile shows a trend consistent with others).

```{r}
#| include: false

# set tau values (aka quantiles or percentiles) here and run model

tauval <- c(.05, .5, .95, .99)
taulab <- c("05th", "50th", "95th", "99th")

quantreg_position_tauval <- rq(age ~ Years.Since.1982*squad_position_name, 
                                data = dfsquads, tau = tauval)



```

```{r}
#| output: true
#| out-width: "100%"

# With only year as predictor, it will be repetitive in the data
# Match to year, grab distinct
pred_tauval <- data.frame(dfsquads %>% select(year, squad_position_name), 
                          quantreg_position_tauval$fitted.values) %>% 
  distinct() 

colnames(pred_tauval) <- c("year", "squad_position_name", taulab)

pred_tauval <- pred_tauval %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    -c(year, squad_position_name),
    names_to = "Percentile", 
    values_to = "age",
  ) %>% 
  arrange(year, Percentile)

# Labels for lines 
line_labels <- pred_tauval %>%
  group_by(Percentile, squad_position_name) %>%
  slice_max(year, n = 1) %>%
  ungroup()

# Label of slopes; year and age determine placement on graph
  # short cut to compute slope from end points rather than map through regression results
  # coef(quantreg_position_tauval)
slope_labels <- pred_tauval %>%
  group_by(Percentile, squad_position_name) %>%
  summarize(
    slope_per_wc = ((age[year == 2026] - age[year == 1982]) / 44)*4,
    age = age[year == 2006], # just for graph placement
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>% 
  mutate(year = 2006,  # just for graph placement
        label = sprintf("%+.3f/WC", slope_per_wc)
        ) %>% 
  # manually tweaking to not have overlap
  mutate(
    age = age +
      recode_values(
        Percentile,
        "99th" ~ 0.70,
        "95th" ~ -0.70,
        "50th" ~ 0,
        "05th" ~ 0
      )
  )

# With all data points, but facet wrap by position
dfsquads %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = age, 
             color = Percentile # not in dfsquads, but matches labels to color
  )) +
  geom_jitter(color = "grey",# palette_green,
              shape = 21, fill = NA,
              height = 0, width = .8, alpha=.3) +
  geom_line(data = pred_tauval, 
            mapping = aes(x = year, y = age, color = Percentile)) +
  facet_wrap(.~squad_position_name) + #, scales = "free_y") + 
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1", 
                     name = "Position") + 
  # Labels by lines instead of legend
  geom_text(
    data = line_labels,
    aes(label = Percentile),
    size = 3.5,
    hjust = -0.1,
    vjust = 0.5,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_label(
    data = slope_labels,
    aes(label = label),
    fill = scales::alpha("white", .75),
    #color = "black",
    size = 3.5,
    linewidth = 0,
    label.padding = unit(.08, "lines"),
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  # To only show actual years in the data
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = sort(unique(dfsquads$year)), 
    guide = guide_axis(angle = 45), 
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, # 0.02)) # extra space on the right
                                .15)) # extra room for labels
  ) +
  labs(title = "Men's World Cup (1982-2026) Player Ages by Position",
       subtitle = "Quantile Regression Fit Lines at Selected Percentiles",
       caption = "Note: Slopes represent change in age per World Cup (every 4 years) for each percentile", 
       x = "Year", y = "Player Age (Years)") + 
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none")
```

Using bootstrapped standard errors and taking into account clustering within squad, we can calculate confidence intervals and significance testing for each of these longevity slopes to test the "location shift of longevity". 

```{r}
#| label: fit-model-slopes_byposition_tauval
#| eval: false

# speed / efficiency:
  # due to processing time during local development: 
  # save the model locally, then in a separate code chunk just load it
  # Only manually rerun this chunk to resave the model if there are changes to the data or this 
    # simply because all these bootstraps take so long

# Slopes by position from regressions from all tauval
  # Small note: Noticed this seems to use df from the full sample for calculating CI
    # Not as ideal as using position specific; but it would still be in the thousands so not practically important
set.seed(123)
slopes_byposition_tauval <- emmeans::emtrends(
  quantreg_position_tauval, ~ squad_position_name | tau,
  var = "Years.Since.1982",
  se = "boot", 
  cluster = dfsquads$team_year_cluster, 
  R = num_boot_sim)


saveRDS(slopes_byposition_tauval,
        file = "slopes_byposition_tauval.rds")

# Predicted values by position from regressions for all tauval
# 2026 corresponds to Years.Since.1982 = 44
set.seed(123)
pred_byposition_tauval <- emmeans::emmeans(
  quantreg_position_tauval,
  specs   = ~ squad_position_name | tau + Years.Since.1982,   # keep year as its own grouping var, not averaged over,
  at      = list(Years.Since.1982 = c(0, 44)), # 1982 and 2026
  se      = "boot",
  cluster = dfsquads$team_year_cluster,
  R       = num_boot_sim
)

saveRDS(pred_byposition_tauval,
        file = "pred_byposition_tauval.rds")

```


```{r}
#| output: true
#| out-width: "100%"


# saved for efficiency, eval: false on its creation, not rendered and must be recreated manually
slopes_byposition_tauval <- readRDS("slopes_byposition_tauval.rds")
pred_byposition_tauval <- readRDS("pred_byposition_tauval.rds")

# slopes by position at each tau into data frame df
slopes_byposition_tauval_df <- summary(slopes_byposition_tauval, infer = c(TRUE, TRUE)) %>% 
  as_tibble() %>% 
    mutate(AgeChangePerWC = Years.Since.1982.trend * 4,
           SEPerWC    = SE * 4,
           lower.CL.PerWC = lower.CL *4,
           upper.CL.PerWC = upper.CL *4,
           Position = squad_position_name) 


# predicted values by position at each tau and for two different years into df
pred_byposition_tauval_df <- summary(pred_byposition_tauval, infer = c(TRUE, TRUE)) %>% 
  as_tibble() %>% 
  filter(round(tau, 2) %in% c(.50, .95, .99)) %>% 
  rename(Position = squad_position_name) %>% 
  mutate(year_label = case_when(
           Years.Since.1982 == 0 ~ "1982", 
           Years.Since.1982 == 44 ~ "2026"),
         tau_label = paste0("\u03c4 = ", sprintf("%.2f", tau))) %>% 
  select(tau_label, Position, year_label, emmean, SE, lower.CL, upper.CL) %>% 
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols     = c(tau_label, Position),
    names_from  = year_label,
    values_from = c(emmean, SE, lower.CL, upper.CL),
    names_glue  = "{.value}_{year_label}"
  )
# columns produced: emmean_1982, emmean_2026, SE_1982, SE_2026,
#                   lower.CL_1982, upper.CL_1982, lower.CL_2026, upper.CL_2026


combined_position_table <- slopes_byposition_tauval_df %>% 
  filter(round(tau, 2) %in% c(.50, .95, .99)) %>% 
  mutate(tau_label = paste0("\u03c4 = ", sprintf("%.2f", tau)) # "τ = 0.95"
         ) %>%   
  left_join(
    pred_byposition_tauval_df,
    by = c("Position", "tau_label")
  ) %>% 
  select(tau_label, Position, AgeChangePerWC, SEPerWC, lower.CL.PerWC, upper.CL.PerWC, p.value,
         emmean_1982, SE_1982, lower.CL_1982, upper.CL_1982,
         emmean_2026, SE_2026, lower.CL_2026, upper.CL_2026) %>% 
  arrange(tau_label, Position)


combined_position_table %>% 
  gt(groupname_col = "tau_label", rowname_col = "Position") %>%
  fmt_number( 
    columns = c(AgeChangePerWC, SEPerWC, lower.CL.PerWC, upper.CL.PerWC),
    decimals = 3
  ) %>% 
    fmt_number( # for pred ages, just 1 decimal
    columns = c(emmean_1982, SE_1982, lower.CL_1982, upper.CL_1982,
                emmean_2026, SE_2026, lower.CL_2026, upper.CL_2026),
    decimals = 1 
  ) %>% 
  fmt(
    columns = p.value, 
    fns = function(x) {
      ifelse(x < .001, "<.001", sub("^0\\.", ".", sprintf("%.3f", x)))
    }
  ) %>% 
  cols_merge(columns = c(lower.CL.PerWC, upper.CL.PerWC), pattern = "[{1}, {2}]") %>% 
  cols_merge(columns = c(lower.CL_1982, upper.CL_1982),   pattern = "[{1}, {2}]") %>% 
  cols_merge(columns = c(lower.CL_2026, upper.CL_2026),   pattern = "[{1}, {2}]") %>% 
  cols_label(
    AgeChangePerWC = "Age Δ /WC",
    SEPerWC        = "SE",
    lower.CL.PerWC = "95% CI",
    p.value        = "p",
    emmean_1982    = "Age",
    SE_1982        = "SE",
    lower.CL_1982  = "95% CI",
    emmean_2026    = "Age",
    SE_2026        = "SE",
    lower.CL_2026  = "95% CI"
  ) %>% 
  tab_spanner(label = "Slope (per WC cycle)", columns = c(AgeChangePerWC, SEPerWC, lower.CL.PerWC, p.value)) %>% 
  tab_spanner(label = "Predicted Age, 1982",    columns = c(emmean_1982, SE_1982, lower.CL_1982)) %>% 
  tab_spanner(label = "Predicted Age, 2026",    columns = c(emmean_2026, SE_2026, lower.CL_2026)) %>% 
  cols_align(
    align   = "center",
    columns = c(AgeChangePerWC, SEPerWC, lower.CL.PerWC, p.value, 
                emmean_1982, SE_1982, lower.CL_1982, 
                emmean_2026, SE_2026, lower.CL_2026)
  ) %>% 
  tab_style(style = cell_text(align = "left"), locations = cells_stub()) %>% 
  tab_header(title    = "Longevity by Position",
             subtitle = paste0("Quantile regression slopes and predicted ages, with clustered bootstrapped SEs (", 
                               num_boot_sim, " resamples)")
             ) %>%
  tab_options(table.align = "left")


```

Only goal keepers and defenders show significant increases in median ages. 

Consistent with the "location shift of longevity", we see that all positions show a significant increase in age at the 95th percentile. (And with hesitancy we can note that all but the small sample size goal keepers show a significant increase at the 99th percentile.) 

To test the differences of the slopes at the median and 95th percentile for each position, we again have the "rough SE-limitation comparisons" issue. We will use the same limitation-acknowledging-approach of not using clustering and bootstrapped resampling for standard errors. With these constraints in mind, we do see tentative support for the "shape shift of longevity" among both forwards and defenders, but not for midfielders and not for the small number of goal keepers.

```{r}
#| output: true
#| out-width: "100%"

tau_pair <- c(.5, .95)

pairwise_wald_byposition_95 <- map_dfr(levels(dfsquads$squad_position_name), function(pos) {
  df_pos   <- dfsquads %>% filter(squad_position_name == pos)
  fit_pair <- rq(age ~ Years.Since.1982, data = df_pos, tau = tau_pair)
  a        <- anova(fit_pair, test = "Wald", joint = FALSE)   # se = "nid", not bootstrapped/clustered — same accepted limitation as before
  tab      <- a$table
  tibble(
    Position = pos,
    F_value  = tab[, ncol(tab) - 1],
    p_value  = tab[, ncol(tab)]
  )
}) %>%
  mutate(p_adj = p.adjust(p_value, method = "holm"))  # correcting across the 4 position tests

# TODO here
pairwise_wald_byposition_95 %>% 
  gt(rowname_col = "Position") %>% 
  fmt_number(
    columns = F_value,
    decimals = 3
  ) %>% 
  fmt(
    columns = c(p_value, p_adj),
    fns = function(x) {
      ifelse(x < .001, 
             "<.001", 
             sub("^0\\.", ".", sprintf("%.3f", x)))
    }
  ) %>% 
  cols_label(
    F_value = "F",
    p_value = "p (raw)",
    p_adj   = "p (Holm-adjusted)"
  ) %>% 
  cols_align(align = "center", columns = c(F_value, p_value, p_adj)) %>% 
  tab_style(style = cell_text(align = "left"), locations = cells_stub()) %>% 
  tab_header(
    title    = "Pairwise Comparisons of Median vs 95th Percentile Slopes, for each Position",
    subtitle = "Wald tests, analytic (nid) SEs \u2014 not bootstrapped or cluster-adjusted"
  ) %>% 
  tab_options(table.align = "left")

```

We can again visualize these changes in the distribution over time, but now separately by position, and interpret them in context with the testing. 

```{r}
#| output: true
#| out-width: "100%"


# Positions by year
ggplot(dfsquads, aes(x=age, y=forcats::fct_rev(factor(year)), # top to bottom
                     group=forcats::fct_rev(factor(year)),
                     fill = factor(after_stat(quantile)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient", calc_ecdf = TRUE,
    quantile_lines = TRUE, quantiles = tauval
  ) + 
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1", 
                    name = "Age Percentiles",
                    breaks = 1:4, # ensure order stays correct
                    labels = taulab) + 
  facet_wrap(.~ squad_position_name) +

       x = "Player Age (Years)", y = "Year") + 
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```


Taken together, it appears that the median age is getting older for defenders but not for forwards, but both defenders and forwards show increasing longevity ("location shift of longevity" based on significant slopes at the 95th percentile) and their oldest players are getting *increasingly* or relatively older ("shape shift of longevity" based on greater slopes at the 95th percentile compared to the median, with limitations in testing). Thus, both of these positions show increases in longevity.

![](age_dist_defender.mp4){controls="1" loop="0"}
![](age_dist_forward.mp4){controls="1" loop="0"}

Midfielders show a "location shift of longevity" (based on significant slopes at the 95th percentile), but that increase in the oldest players is not growing at rate significantly greater than their (not-significant) change at the median (that is, not strong support for a "shape shift of longevity"). Thus, we see some slight increases in older midfielders, but not as much support for increasing or unusual minority of particularly long lasting players — a bit of a lack of support for the full ideas of longevity increases.

![](age_dist_midfielder.mp4){controls="1" loop="0"}

The results for the goal keepers are a bit ambiguous, at least in part due to their smaller sample size, but perhaps also because they showed different patterns of age even in the beginning of the expansion era. In terms of pure coefficient size, they had the largest "location shift of longevity" with the largest increase at median ages and the second largest increase at the 95th percentile. But their oldest players were *not* getting *increasingly* or relatively older (no "shape shift of longevity" because their 95th percentile slope did not significantly differ from the median). However, goal keepers *already* had the largest gap between their median and 95th percentile values starting all the way back in the 1980s. (This can also be visually confirmed with the graph "Quantile Regression Fit Lines at Selected Percentiles".) That is, earlier on they already had more of a right tail stretched distribution or shape difference compared to other positions, there were already a lot of exceptionally older goal keepers and their trends over time are, arguably, not increasing that stretch but may be maintaining it. Thus, goal keepers already had exceptional longevity and a different shape, but it may not be accelerating (or we may frame it as other positions seem to be catching up or beginning to get distributions of age shaped more like goal keeper's distributions).  

![](age_dist_goal_keeper.mp4){controls="1" loop="0"}


:::

Overall, there is some support for longevity shape shifting increases among defenders and forwards, a lack of support for any exceptional longevity for midfielders (no shape shifting, but just some overall location shifting at the upper percentile), and ambiguous results for the already-older and smaller sample size of goal keepers. But ultimately, a position analysis was trying to assess if the story of overall increases in longevity in both location shift and shape shift were misleading and just being driven by a goal keepers, and we can definitively say that is not the case, and at least forwards and defenders are contributing.

But what about the alternative explanation that it may just be that teams in the expanding formats select older players? 

# Ruling out alternative explanations: Different squad choices because of different teams?


## Expanding field of teams? 

As the World Cup has expanded, perhaps it is the additional teams who make different selections — for example, teams who rarely get to go to the World Cup may reward veterans who have stuck with their national program but have rarely or never been able to play in a World Cup. One fairly straightforward way to investigate claims about different "types" of teams making different age selections would be to think separately about the more traditional or "core" teams (those who frequently qualify for the World Cup) and the "non-core" teams who are either newly or rarely appearing in World Cup tournaments. Essentially, do the location and especially shape shift of longevity hold true for both types of teams?

While only Brazil has qualified for all 23 World Cups, since 1930 there are 10 teams with at least 15 appearances that I will define as the "core" teams.^[Note that for this analysis, Germany's number of appearances is counted by including teams of Germany (1934-1938; 1994-present) and West Germany (1954-1990), and they are considered a "core" team. In contrast, no later country is connected to Yugoslavia nor the Soviet Union for purposes of counting its total appearances given that each split into many countries, i.e., Yugoslavia's 9 appearances through 1998 are not added to Croatia's 7 appearances since (and overlapping with) 1998, so Croatia is a "non-core" team.] The "core" teams account for 180 squads (appearances of a team in a particular year) in the expansion era of the World Cup. The remaining 74 "non-core" teams participating in the expansion era account for 353 squads (appearances of team per year), including 15 teams with single appearances.^[Note that two of these were not typical single appearances: "Serbia and Montenegro" qualified as a team in one tournament after the break of up Yugoslavia but before the two separated; similarly, Slovakia has qualified once since the break up of Czechslovakia separated it from Czech Republic.]
